questions.title: What is the difference between primitive and reference types in how they are stored, copied, and compared?
questions.tldr: Primitive types (string, number, boolean, undefined, null, symbol, bigint) store immutable raw values directly on the Stack and compare by value. Reference types (Object, Array, Function, Map, Set) store pointers on the Stack to mutable objects allocated on the Heap, comparing by memory address.

questions.title: What does typeof do, and why does typeof null return "object"?
questions.tldr: typeof returns a string indicating the primitive data type of an operand. typeof null returns "object" due to a historic bug in the original 1995 JS engine where null's type tag bit vector (0x00) matched the type tag for objects.

questions.title: What is the difference between null, undefined, and an undeclared variable?
questions.tldr: undefined represents a variable declared but not yet assigned a value; null is an intentional assignment representing empty/no object value; undeclared is a variable that has never been declared in any accessible scope, throwing a ReferenceError on access.

questions.title: What is NaN, why is NaN !== NaN, and how do Number.isNaN() and Object.is() differ from ===?
questions.tldr: NaN ("Not-a-Number") represents an invalid numerical operation result. Per IEEE 754 floating-point standard, NaN is not equal to anything including itself. Number.isNaN() strictly checks if a value is NaN without coercion, unlike global isNaN() which coercively converts to number first.

questions.title: What are truthy and falsy values, and what are all the falsy values in JavaScript?
questions.tldr: In boolean contexts (e.g., if conditions), values are coerced to true (truthy) or false (falsy). There are exactly 8 falsy values in JS: false, 0, -0, 0n (BigInt zero), "" (empty string), null, undefined, and NaN.

questions.title: What is type coercion (implicit vs explicit), and how does == differ from ===?
questions.tldr: Implicit coercion automatically converts types behind the scenes during operations, while explicit coercion is manual conversion by the developer. Strict equality (===) checks both value and type without coercion, whereas loose equality (==) coerces operands to a common type before comparing.

questions.title: How do &&, ||, ??, and ?. work, and what is short-circuit evaluation?
questions.tldr: Short-circuit evaluation means logical expressions evaluate left-to-right and stop as soon as the outcome is guaranteed. && returns the first falsy operand (or last value), || returns the first truthy operand (or last value), ?? returns right operand ONLY if left is null/undefined, and ?. safely short-circuits property access if left is nullish.

questions.title: What are JavaScript's key characteristics (dynamically typed, single-threaded, garbage-collected, multi-paradigm), and how is it related to ECMAScript?
questions.tldr: JS is a dynamically typed, single-threaded, garbage-collected, multi-paradigm language. ECMAScript is the standard specification (ECMA-262); JavaScript is the primary language implementation of that specification.

questions.title: What is a JavaScript engine (e.g., V8), what happens between writing code and running it (parsing, AST, bytecode interpreter, JIT-optimized machine code), and is JavaScript interpreted, compiled, or both?
questions.tldr: V8 parses JS code into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), executes bytecode via an interpreter (Ignition), and dynamically compiles hot code paths into machine code via JIT compilers (TurboFan). JS uses Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation, making it both interpreted and compiled at runtime.

questions.title: What is the difference between the JavaScript engine and the runtime environment (browser vs Node.js), what does "single-threaded" actually mean, and what are the parts of the runtime (memory heap, call stack, Web APIs/libuv, task queues, event loop)?
questions.tldr: The JS engine (e.g. V8) executes ECMAScript code using a Call Stack and Memory Heap. The Runtime Environment (Browser/Node.js) wraps the engine with event loops, task queues, and APIs (Web APIs or libuv) to enable non-blocking asynchronous operation.

questions.title: What is an execution context, what happens in its creation (memory) phase and execution phase, what is a lexical environment, and how does the call stack manage global and function execution contexts?
questions.tldr: An Execution Context (EC) is an environment created when running JS code. It consists of a Memory Creation Phase (hoisting variables and functions) and an Execution Phase (running code line by line). The Call Stack manages active ECs on a LIFO basis.

questions.title: How is memory managed in JavaScript (stack vs heap, garbage collection via mark-and-sweep and reachability), and what causes memory leaks (closures, forgotten event listeners, timers)?
questions.tldr: Memory is managed automatically via Mark-and-Sweep garbage collection, which reclaims memory from objects unattached from root references. Memory leaks occur when unreachable objects are unintentionally retained by active references (e.g., closures, timers, event listeners).

questions.title: What is the difference between var, let, and const in scope, redeclaration, and reassignment, and can a const object be modified?
questions.tldr: var is function-scoped, hoisted with undefined, and allows redeclaration. let and const are block-scoped ({}), hoisted into the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ), and disallow redeclaration. const prevents reassigning the variable reference, but object properties inside a const object can still be mutated.

questions.title: What are global, function, block, and lexical scope, and how do the scope chain and variable shadowing work?
questions.tldr: Scope determines variable accessibility. Global scope is root; function scope is bound inside function bodies; block scope is bound within {} pairs. Lexical scope means inner functions resolve variables based on where they were written in source code, forming a scope chain.

questions.title: What is hoisting, how do var, let/const, function declarations, and function expressions each behave, and what is the Temporal Dead Zone?
questions.tldr: Hoisting is JS allocating memory for variable/function declarations before executing code. var hoists initialized to undefined; let/const hoist into the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) throwing ReferenceError if accessed early; function declarations hoist fully.

questions.title: What are first-class functions, higher-order functions, and callback functions?
questions.tldr: First-class functions mean functions are treated like regular values (stored in variables, passed as args, returned from functions). Higher-order functions accept or return other functions. Callback functions are passed as arguments to be executed later.

questions.title: What is the difference between function declarations, function expressions, and arrow functions, including whether arrow functions have their own this and arguments and whether they can be constructors?
questions.tldr: Function declarations are hoisted fully; expressions are bound to variables. Arrow functions have concise syntax, lexical this (inherited from outer scope), no arguments object, no prototype property, and cannot be used as constructors with new.

questions.title: What are rest parameters, spread syntax, default parameters, and the arguments object?
questions.tldr: Rest parameters (...args) collect remaining function arguments into an array. Spread syntax (...arr) expands iterables into elements. Default parameters specify fallbacks for undefined. arguments is an array-like object in regular functions.

questions.title: What is a closure, how does it work, and what are its practical uses (including IIFEs)?
questions.tldr: A closure is a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment, allowing inner functions to access outer variables even after the outer function has finished executing.

questions.title: What is a pure function, and what is a side effect?
questions.tldr: A pure function given the same inputs will always return the exact same output without causing side effects (modifying global state, mutating args, or performing external I/O).

questions.title: What are currying and function composition?
questions.tldr: Currying transforms a multi-argument function into a sequence of unary functions. Function composition combines multiple functions where the output of one function becomes the input of the next.

questions.title: How is the value of this determined: default binding (and the effect of strict mode), implicit binding, explicit binding, new, and arrow functions?
questions.tldr: this is determined by how a function is called: default binding (global/undefined in strict mode), implicit binding (object calling method), explicit binding (call/apply/bind), new binding (new object created), or lexical binding (arrow functions).

questions.title: What happens to this when a method is passed as a callback, and how do you fix it?
questions.tldr: When a method is passed as a callback, it loses its original implicit object binding (defaulting to window/undefined). Fix it by explicitly binding with .bind(), wrapping in an arrow function, or passing an inline callback.

questions.title: What is the difference between call(), apply(), and bind()?
questions.tldr: call() invokes the function immediately with this and individual arguments. apply() invokes immediately with this and an array of arguments. bind() returns a new permanently bound function without invoking it immediately.

questions.title: How are objects created and accessed (dot vs bracket notation), how does destructuring work for objects and arrays, and what do Object.keys(), Object.values(), and Object.entries() do?
questions.tldr: Objects are created via literals {}, Object.create(), or constructors. Properties are accessed via dot or bracket notation. Destructuring extracts values into variables. Object.keys/values/entries return arrays of own enumerable property keys, values, or [key, value] pairs.

questions.title: What is the difference between a shallow and a deep copy, and what are the limitations of spread, Object.assign(), JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)), and structuredClone()?
questions.tldr: Shallow copy duplicates top-level properties but retains shared references to nested objects. Deep copy duplicates all levels recursively. Spread and Object.assign create shallow copies; JSON.parse/stringify fails on functions/Date/undefined/circular refs; structuredClone() performs true deep cloning natively.

questions.title: What are object mutation and immutability, and why does Object.freeze() not deeply freeze an object?
questions.tldr: Object.freeze() makes an object shallowly immutable (prevents adding, deleting, or modifying top-level properties). It is shallow; nested objects remain mutable unless recursively frozen.

questions.title: What is the prototype chain, how does prototypal inheritance work, and what is the difference between prototype and \_\_proto\_\_?
questions.tldr: Every JS object has an internal prototype link to another object. Prototypal inheritance allows objects to inherit properties/methods via this chain. .prototype is the object attached to constructor functions; __proto__ is the internal accessor link on object instances.

questions.title: What happens internally when new is used, and how do constructor functions and Object.create() relate to it?
questions.tldr: When new Fn() is called: 1) A new empty object is created, 2) Its __proto__ is linked to Fn.prototype, 3) Fn is executed with this set to the new object, 4) The object is returned (unless Fn returns its own explicit object).

questions.title: How do classes relate to prototypes, and how do extends, super, static methods, method overriding, getters/setters, and #private fields work?
questions.tldr: ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over prototypal inheritance. extends sets up prototype links; super calls parent constructor/methods; static methods belong to the class itself; #private fields are encapsulated at runtime.

questions.title: When would you use a Map or Set instead of an object or array, and how do you remove duplicates from an array with a Set?
questions.tldr: Map accepts keys of any data type and maintains insertion order. Set stores unique values of any type. Use Set with Array.from() or spread to remove array duplicates in O(N) time.

questions.title: When would you use map(), filter(), reduce(), forEach(), find(), some(), and every(), and how do they differ?
questions.tldr: map transforms elements returning a new array; filter returns items passing a test; reduce accumulates elements into a single value; forEach iterates with side effects (returns undefined); find returns first matching element; some/every check boolean conditions.

questions.title: Which array methods mutate the original array, including slice() vs splice(), the numeric sort() pitfall, flat(), and the non-mutating toSorted() and toReversed()?
questions.tldr: Mutating methods modify original array in place (push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse). Non-mutating methods return new arrays (slice, concat, map, filter, toSorted, toReversed). Array.prototype.sort() converts elements to strings by default!

questions.title: What is the difference between for...in and for...of?
questions.tldr: for...in iterates over enumerable property keys of an object (including prototype chain). for...of iterates over values of iterable objects (Arrays, Strings, Maps, Sets).

questions.title: How do try/catch/finally work, and when would you create a custom Error class?
questions.tldr: try runs code; catch captures thrown exceptions; finally always runs regardless of outcome. Custom error classes extend built-in Error to add custom properties (e.g., statusCode).

questions.title: How does the event loop work, what is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks, why do Promise callbacks run before setTimeout(fn, 0), and what happens when the call stack is busy?
questions.tldr: The Event Loop monitors Call Stack and Queues. When Call Stack is empty, it processes ALL Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) before processing ONE Macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O). A busy call stack blocks the event loop and freezes the UI.

questions.title: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
questions.tldr: Concurrency is dealing with multiple tasks at once by interleaving execution on a single core (Event Loop). Parallelism is executing multiple tasks simultaneously at the exact same physical instant on multiple CPU cores.

questions.title: What is callback hell, what are the limitations of callbacks, and why were Promises introduced?
questions.tldr: Callback hell refers to deeply nested, unmaintainable asynchronous callbacks ("pyramid of doom"). Promises were introduced to flatten async flows into chainable, composable pipelines with centralized error handling.

questions.title: What is a Promise, what are its three states, and what do .then(), .catch(), and .finally() do?
questions.tldr: A Promise represents the eventual completion or failure of an async operation. It has 3 states: Pending, Fulfilled, or Rejected. .then() handles fulfillment, .catch() handles rejection, and .finally() executes regardless.

questions.title: How does Promise chaining work when a .then() callback returns a value, returns another Promise, or throws an error?
questions.tldr: In Promise chaining, returning a primitive/object wraps it in a resolved Promise; returning another Promise waits for it to resolve; throwing an error or returning a rejected Promise skips to the nearest .catch().

questions.title: What do Promise.resolve() and Promise.reject() do, and what is the difference between Promise.all(), allSettled(), race(), and any()?
questions.tldr: Promise.all waits for all to succeed (fails fast on first error); allSettled waits for all to finish regardless of outcome; race resolves/rejects as soon as the FIRST promise settles; any resolves as soon as the FIRST promise succeeds (fails if all fail).

questions.title: What does an async function return, and how is await related to Promises?
questions.tldr: An async function always returns a Promise. The await operator pauses execution inside the async function until the awaited Promise settles, unwrapping its resolved value.

questions.title: How do you handle errors with async/await, and what is an unhandled Promise rejection?
questions.tldr: Handle errors in async/await using try/catch blocks or appending .catch() to the async call. Unhandled promise rejections occur when a rejected promise has no handler, triggering process.on('unhandledRejection') or browser warnings.

questions.title: Why doesn't await work as expected inside forEach(), and what is the difference between sequential and parallel awaits?
questions.tldr: forEach runs callbacks synchronously without awaiting them, firing requests concurrently without waiting. Use for...of for sequential awaits, and Promise.all() with map() for parallel awaits.

questions.title: How do async race conditions cause stale results, and how do AbortController and AbortSignal cancel in-flight requests to prevent them?
questions.tldr: Async race conditions happen when responses return out of order. AbortController creates an AbortSignal to cancel pending HTTP requests when new requests are triggered.

questions.title: What is the DOM, and how does JavaScript interact with it?
questions.tldr: The DOM (Document Object Model) is a tree-structure object representation of an HTML document created by the browser, allowing JS to read and manipulate page structure, content, and styling.

questions.title: How do event bubbling, capturing, and delegation work, and what are the differences between event.target and event.currentTarget, and between preventDefault() and stopPropagation()?
questions.tldr: Event propagation has 3 phases: Capturing (down from window to target), Target, and Bubbling (up from target to window). Event delegation attaches one listener to a parent. target is element clicked; currentTarget is element with listener.

questions.title: What is the difference between innerHTML, innerText, and textContent, and what is the XSS risk with innerHTML?
questions.tldr: innerHTML parses and returns HTML tags (vulnerable to XSS). textContent returns raw unformatted text of all nodes. innerText returns visible rendered text (triggers layout recalculation).

questions.title: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies, how do XSS and CSRF differ as risks, and what do the HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite cookie flags do?
questions.tldr: localStorage persists until manually cleared (5MB); sessionStorage persists until tab closes (5MB); cookies send with HTTP requests (4KB). HttpOnly cookies prevent XSS theft; SameSite mitigates CSRF.

questions.title: What does fetch() return (the Response object), why doesn't it reject on 4xx/5xx errors and how do you check response.ok, how are credentials sent, and what is CORS and why does it exist?
questions.tldr: fetch() returns a Promise resolving to a Response object. It does NOT reject on 4xx/5xx HTTP status codes (check response.ok). CORS is a browser security mechanism blocking cross-origin requests unless server headers allow it.

questions.title: What is the difference between ES modules and CommonJS?
questions.tldr: CommonJS (module.exports / require) is synchronous, used in traditional Node.js, and evaluated at runtime. ES Modules (import / export) are asynchronous, statically analyzed at compile-time (enabling tree-shaking), and native to modern JS.

questions.title: Predict the output of a var hoisting example and explain why.
questions.tldr: `var` declarations are hoisted to the top of their enclosing function/global scope and initialized with `undefined`, whereas function declarations are hoisted along with their full implementation. Statements inside unexecuted conditional blocks still hoist `var` variable declarations.

questions.title: Predict the output of a closure inside a loop and explain why.
questions.tldr: Using `var` in a loop creates a single shared function-scoped variable binding. When `setTimeout` callbacks run asynchronously after loop completion, all closures reference the final mutated value (`3, 3, 3`). Using `let` creates a new block-scoped binding per iteration (`0, 1, 2`).

questions.title: Predict the output of this with regular vs arrow functions.
questions.tldr: Regular functions evaluate `this` dynamically at invocation time based on *how* they are called. Arrow functions do NOT have their own `this`; they capture `this` lexically from their enclosing parent scope at definition time.

questions.title: Predict the output of Promise + setTimeout() code and explain the event loop.
questions.tldr: Synchronous script execution completes first $

questions.title: Predict the output of async/await + Promise code and explain microtask behavior.
questions.tldr: An `async` function executes synchronously up to the first `await` expression. The expression following `await` is evaluated synchronously, while the code after `await` is wrapped into a Microtask and paused until the awaited Promise resolves.

questions.title: Find and fix the bug in async code that uses await inside forEach(), leaves a Promise rejection unhandled, or shows stale results because of a race condition.
questions.tldr: `Array.prototype.forEach` does NOT await Promises returned by its callback; it triggers async operations concurrently without waiting. Use `for...of` for sequential execution, `Promise.all()` for parallel execution, `try/catch` for error handling, and `AbortController` for race conditions.

questions.title: Find and fix the bug in code that loses this in a callback or reads a stale closure value.
questions.tldr: Detaching an object method and passing it as a callback loses its implicit `this` context binding (`this` defaults to `undefined` or `window`). Closed-over variables inside long-lived callbacks (timers, event handlers) capture initial variable snapshots (stale closures).

questions.title: Implement Array.prototype.reduce() from scratch (handling empty arrays and missing initialValue).
questions.tldr: `Array.prototype.reduce` executes a reducer callback across every element, accumulating a single return value. If `initialValue` is omitted, the first element becomes the accumulator and iteration starts at index 1. Calling it on an empty array without an initial value throws a `TypeError`.

questions.title: Implement debounce() and explain exactly how it works.
questions.tldr: `debounce` delays function execution until a specified quiet period has elapsed since the last invocation. Every incoming trigger clears the active timer and schedules a new one, suppressing rapid event bursts (e.g. search inputs, window resize).

questions.title: Implement throttle() and explain the difference from debounce.
questions.tldr: `throttle` ensures a function executes at most once per specified time interval, providing steady, periodic execution during continuous events (e.g. scrolling, mouse movement). While `debounce` waits for silence, `throttle` guarantees a regulated execution rate.

questions.title: Implement Promise.all() from scratch (order preservation, fast-reject).
questions.tldr: `Promise.all(promises)` takes an array/iterable of promises and returns a single Promise that resolves to an array of results in the **exact original order** when all input promises fulfill, or rejects immediately with the reason of the first rejected promise (fail-fast).

questions.title: Implement memoize() and explain how closures make it work.
questions.tldr: `memoize` caches the return values of expensive pure functions based on their serialized arguments using a closure-scoped `Map`. Subsequent calls with identical arguments skip computation and return the cached result in $O(1)$ time.

questions.title: Implement an EventEmitter with on(), off(), once(), and emit().
questions.tldr: An `EventEmitter` implements the Publish-Subscribe pattern. It maintains an internal map of event names to listener arrays (`Map<string, Function[]>`) to register (`on`), trigger (`emit`), remove (`off`), and execute one-time handlers (`once`).

questions.title: Implement a deep-clone utility (and explain structuredClone vs JSON.parse/stringify limitations).
questions.tldr: Deep cloning creates a completely independent copy of nested objects and arrays. An interview-optimal deep clone checks for primitives, detects circular references using a `WeakMap`, and recursively clones object and array properties.

questions.title: What are the time complexities of common JavaScript built-ins (push/pop vs shift/unshift, includes/indexOf, Map/Set lookups, sort, string concatenation), and why do they matter when solving problems?
questions.tldr: Array `push`/`pop` operate in $O(1)$ amortized time. `shift`/`unshift` operate in $O(n)$ time due to memory element re-indexing. `includes`/`indexOf` are $O(n)$ linear scans. `Map`/`Set` operations are $O(1)$ amortized lookups. `Array.prototype.sort()` is $O(n \log n)$ (V8 Timsort).

questions.title: LeetCode 1: Two Sum — Find two indices whose values sum to target using a hash map lookup vs brute-force nested loops.
questions.tldr: Pattern: Hash Map Complement Lookup. | Mnemonic: "Don't search forward for a pair; store the past and look back for the complement in $O(1)$."

questions.title: LeetCode 242: Valid Anagram — Check whether two strings are anagrams using a 26-element frequency array vs string sorting.
questions.tldr: Pattern: 26-Element Fixed Frequency Array. | Mnemonic: "If character counts cancel to zero, they are anagrams."

questions.title: LeetCode 49: Group Anagrams — Group an array of strings into anagram clusters using sorted string keys vs frequency string hashing in a Map.
questions.tldr: Pattern: Canonical Key Hashing with Map. | Mnemonic: "All anagrams share the same sorted canonical signature or frequency string."

questions.title: LeetCode 387: First Unique Character in a String — Find the index of the first non-repeating character using two-pass counting vs quadratic scanning.
questions.tldr: Pattern: Two-Pass Frequency Counting. | Mnemonic: "Count in pass 1; identify the earliest count of 1 in pass 2."

questions.title: LeetCode 349: Intersection of Two Arrays — Find the intersection of two arrays returning unique elements using a Set vs linear includes scan.
questions.tldr: Pattern: Set Membership & In-Place Deletion. | Mnemonic: "Load smaller array into a Set; delete as you match to enforce uniqueness."

questions.title: LeetCode 125: Valid Palindrome — Check whether a string is a palindrome with two pointers and in-place ASCII character skips vs built-in reverse string allocations.
questions.tldr: Pattern: Two Pointers Inward Traversal. | Mnemonic: "Meet in the middle while skipping non-alphanumerics."

questions.title: LeetCode 151: Reverse Words in a String — Reverse words in a string, trim whitespace, and reduce multiple spaces to a single space.
questions.tldr: Pattern: Regex Tokenization & Reversal. | Mnemonic: "Trim ends, split on whitespace chunks `/\s+/`, reverse, and join."

questions.title: LeetCode 283: Move Zeroes — Move all zeros to the end of an array in place while preserving order using read/write pointers vs extra array buffers.
questions.tldr: Pattern: Same-Direction Read/Write Pointers. | Mnemonic: "Read every element; swap non-zeros forward into the write index."

questions.title: LeetCode 88: Merge Sorted Array — Merge two sorted arrays into nums1 in-place from back to front using 3 pointers vs array copy and sort.
questions.tldr: Pattern: 3-Pointer Back-to-Front In-Place Merge. | Mnemonic: "Start from the back where the empty space lives."

questions.title: LeetCode 3: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters — Find the longest substring without repeating characters using dynamic sliding window with Map index jumping vs brute-force substring scanning.
questions.tldr: Pattern: Dynamic Sliding Window with Last-Seen Index Map. | Mnemonic: "Expand right; on duplicate, jump left forward past its earlier position."

questions.title: LeetCode 20: Valid Parentheses — Check whether a string of brackets is valid using a LIFO array stack vs quadratic string replacement.
questions.tldr: Pattern: LIFO Stack Matching. | Mnemonic: "The most recently opened bracket must be closed first."

questions.title: LeetCode 232: Implement Queue using Stacks — Implement a FIFO queue using two LIFO array stacks with amortized O(1) operations.
questions.tldr: Pattern: Two Stacks (`inStack` & `outStack`) with Lazy Reversal. | Mnemonic: "Push to inStack; transfer to outStack only when outStack is empty."
